#7356. Election season lifted public radio sites. So did a Supreme Court scandal and license plate drama.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of New Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story. Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

“But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said.

“[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”

BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp

— Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026

WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

“We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”

“Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said.

Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”

The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

“We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”

And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”

“I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”

If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

“The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”

Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

“Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

“We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”

Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

#7355. Senior Product Marketing Manager [IC4] at Sourcegraph

Our mission is to bring clarity and control to the world's most complex codebases. AI is accelerating code creation, but the infrastructure to understand, oversee, and evolve that code hasn't kept pace. Sourcegraph gives engineering organizations full visibility across their systems, precise context for their agents, and the ability to execute coordinated code changes at scale. From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been yet another busy week. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

The Chicago Sun-Times announced a new slogan this week. What is it?

“Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

“The union has been negotiating a new contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”

A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

“Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”

Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government plans to scrap public media license fees.

#7349. I Blind-Tested 3 Gemini Models On Real SEO Questions – Neon Won 5 Of 6 via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Is the newest AI model actually better, or do we just assume it is? My blind test of three Gemini models gave a clear answer.

Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

The blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

My Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:

Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week plan that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:

What stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

My revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):

Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

At first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a big jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active users, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:

And those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.

#7348. An open laptop, a crowded Orange Line train, and a tipster

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

ProPublica says November has been the busiest month ever for its tips line.

Is “seen on the Orange Line” the new “overheard on the Acela”?

RELATED ARTICLEProPublica wanted to find more sources in the federal government. So it brought a truck.Neel DhaneshaMarch 31, 2025ProPublica reported on potential plans to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.”

But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece:

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer.

Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint.

Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip.

“That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.”

We’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting.

ProPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera said. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line.

RELATED ARTICLEHow to leak to a journalistLaura Hazard OwenApril 2, 2025“We have to attribute some of this surge to our efforts to get out into the world and show people that we’re listening and that they can trust us with their knowledge — from working with ad companies in Washington, D.C., to get our tips line on bus shelters, to flyering outside of conferences, and events with sources that could help our reporting needs,” she said.

During a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by.

“We’re always looking for ways to reach the people we need to reach, in the places they’re likeliest to be, based on our reporting needs,” Mel Kramer, engagement team product manager, said. “A good tips line is both staffed and comes to mind quickly. When someone sees something that investigative reporters should see, we want them to think of ProPublica.”

Up next for the team? Handing out coasters in sports bars to collect info on sports betting.

#7345. Newsletters, obits, and the world’s longest yard sale: How some local news sites saw their traffic spike

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

It’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

Today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in New York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

W42ST In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. In New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

Publisher Phil O’Brien said that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

“A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”

O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s currently trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said.

Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski.

The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

“We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”

Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

Similarweb stats showed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said.

In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said.

In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”

The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

#7342. Reddit’s AEO Tool Recommendations Have A Promoter Problem via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

An analysis of subreddits flagged most users weighing in on AEO tools as likely promoters. Among the rest, accuracy was the top feature complaint.

Graphite flagged 55% of the users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool across 54 subreddits this year as likely working for or promoting a marketing software product.

Among the users it didn’t flag, the accuracy of visibility scores drew more unfavorable opinions than any other product feature.

The growth agency picked subreddits where AEO comes up regularly and found 5,990 posts and 25,392 comments from January through September that mention a tool. OpenAI language models labeled the mentions, the opinions and the likely promoters.

The agency helps companies with AEO and SEO and says it doesn’t sell AEO tools or accept payment to be mentioned. Its CEO, Ethan Smith, is an investor in Peec AI, one of three tools tied for the highest score in the analysis.

Graphite flagged 1,298 of the 2,365 Reddit users who gave an opinion of an AEO tool or a marketing platform’s AEO features.

A user was flagged when the agency’s model put the chance at 50% or more that their posts promoted a marketing product they build, own, work for, sell or partner with. That includes SEO, AEO, sales and web analytics tools. An agency’s description of its own client work did not constitute promotion.

To test the model, the company manually inspected 43 of the users it had flagged. Ultimately, 12% of them disclosed being promoters, while 62% were found to have promoted a product but failed to identify themselves as such; the remaining ones were judged non-promoters. The write-up also says that some of the models’ labeling decisions could be incorrect.

Four types of likely promoter Reddit accounts were identified. Each type exhibited a pattern across several posts or comments.

One account was used to recommend the same lesser-known tracking service on eight posts and comments. In January this user claimed that they switched from a competitor, and 11 days later they commented about possibly purchasing the product.

Another account made reference to a little-known product in four comments with well-known tracking services over the course of eight days.

A third account posted three separate times for the same product within 12 minutes.

Over six weeks, 38 accounts recommended the same product in 52 comments, each using the phrase “from what I’ve read” in its recommendation. That phrase appears with any other tool no more than twice.

Of the opinions regarding the accuracy of AEO tools from users who weren’t flagged, 143 were negative while 27 had positive views. No other feature elicited as many negative opinions. These users provided opinions on 44 tools, for a total of 1,557 opinions.

Graphite’s chart compares praise and criticism across features after excluding opinions from users it flagged as likely promoters.

According to the write-up, users frequently view visibility scores as estimates due to variation in AI answers among different runs, locations and users. Several have advised fellow users to “treat them as trend, not truth” and to verify the information through manual review.

The citation data, or the citations used by AI systems as source material for their answers, was generally viewed positively by users. Price received more user opinions than any other attribute and most of those opinions were negative, at 182 negative versus 98 positive.

The agency also evaluated the 11 tools which generated sufficient opinions using a 0-100 point scale; a score of 50 represented neutral. Each of the 11 tools scored between 54 and 66 points. The authors also said the ranges around many of the tools’ scores overlapped and therefore, the differences in scores could lack statistical significance.

Graphite’s count puts a number on how many Reddit users weighing in on AEO tools may be promoting marketing software. Before a tool recommended on Reddit goes on your shortlist, check the account’s history for repeat plugs and a story that changes from post to post.

Graphite’s tool scores reflect opinions from January through September, and the company says their order could change as more opinions come in. Complaints about the accuracy of visibility scores give you something to test before renewing. Run a sample of your tracked prompts by hand and compare the results with the tool’s numbers.

#7340. Confident kids, cautious elders: What we get wrong (and right) about who really understands social media algorithms

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in New Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

Surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

The self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

In other words, the generational edge that shows up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

To capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

Then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

Exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger users, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

My data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It shows up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

Third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest users are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and says they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University.

#7336. The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Many publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

One of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

As part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

“As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” said Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”

The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent company, News Corp.

“We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”

Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

Many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the company’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

“One of the most important issues for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”

More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

Many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

Known Agents currently tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

“Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” said King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”

King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

“It’s been such a manual process,” said King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”

Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the company’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

“We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, said. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”

Lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he said.

Slate currently has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

“It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” said Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google is bringing together its products and services in a way that could fundamentally change what it means to do SEO.

Google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature. The expansion unifies many of Google’s disparate products and services into a single personalized search experience. This update represents a profound change to Google’s Search experience and is likely among the most consequential changes to SEO.

Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:

“The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we’re introducing more personally relevant responses, so it’s easier to find just what you need.”

Some SEOs objected to characterizing Personal Intelligence as something that is about Search, explaining that Personal Intelligence is about Gemini, AI Mode, and AI Overviews. That view can be justified because Google’s announcement is somewhat ambiguous.

Google’s announcement uses the upper-case word Search sixteen times. That seems to be a clear signal that Personal Intelligence affects Search.

“A more tailored Google Search that’s uniquely yours…

…Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence…

…bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”

The following passage seems to unambiguously paint the rollout as affecting Search:

“Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”

The above passage clearly separates AI Mode from Search. Yet, other passages reference AI Mode in Search, introducing a certain amount of ambiguity. An argument can be made that this does not affect Search, but there’s a strong counter-argument there, too.

Google’s announcement ties AI Overviews and AI Mode responses to recent Search contexts, meaning that contextual data from Search can be shared to AIO and AI Mode:

“You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context.”

And in another passage Google explains that the contextual data from the Gemini App can be shared with AI Mode in Search:

“In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.”

“So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.”

So it looks like the context data flows from Search to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as from the Gemini App to AI Mode in Search.

The announcement identifies six connected apps:

But Personal Intelligence is about a whole lot more. It’s about the transformation of disparate services and products into what Google CEO, Sundar Pichai, described in October 2026 as one unified search experience that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

“I expect our agents to provide that unifying experience across these products. In fact, that agentic layer, rather than try to converge or think about different products and how they come together, I think the agentic layer naturally ends up doing that, right?

Because your agents, they’re running in the cloud, they’re running 24/7, they have your context. And so they can pick up things where you left off.

So you can start a task in some place. You go to the other place. Your agent has that context for you.

So I think the agentic layer offers us a chance to bring a unified product experience better than ever before.”

Google’s Personal Intelligence was first announced as a paid Gemini App beta feature in January 2026, which was expanded to AI Mode in search about a week later, initially supporting Gmail and Google Photos as an opt-in Search Labs experiment.

In March it was expanded to free tier users in the United States and within a few months it was available in 200 countries and 98 languages.

Google announced the expansion of the range of information AI Mode can draw on through Personal Intelligence so that now it includes Google Wallet data, files stored in Google Drive, and Gemini conversations. Google also announced increased personalization of AI Overviews and AI Mode based on recent search activity.

Opt-in connectivity of Google Wallet to AI Mode is beginning to roll out. This is really big and ties into Sundar Pichai’s vision of Search becoming increasingly focused on helping users accomplish tasks. Google Wallet aggregates data from linked accounts like Gmail and partner apps.

Google Wallet affects travel (like airline tickets), finance, commerce, event tickets, plus sensitive data (in some regions) like drivers license, and health insurance cards. When this feature is enabled, Google Wallet automatically scans incoming emails to import boarding passes, event tickets, loyalty cards, and shipping updates.

Now all of that is connected with Personal Intelligence.

Connectivity to AI Mode is coming in the next few weeks. Google announced that connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence will enable AI Mode to pull information from across stored Google Drive documents, spreadsheets, and PDFs to provide personalized responses and assist users with projects, planning, and decision-making.

“With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation plan ahead of tax season.”

Personal Intelligence will be sharing Gemini conversational context between the Gemini app and AI Mode within the next few weeks. Search personalization will come in the form of more personally relevant responses based on recent search activity.

Personalization transparency is coming soon. Users will be able to see what personal context AI Mode used to generate a response and correct that information.

Transformation Of Google Search Personal Intelligence represents a fundamental change in how Google Search (and/or AI Mode in Search) can respond to users, incorporating knowledge about their activities alongside information from the web.

Unification Of Google’s Products And Services Previously disparate Google products and services are now increasingly part of a unified, personalized search experience.

Google’s Agentic Layer The expansion of Personal Intelligence is consistent with Sundar Pichai’s vision of a unified, task-based experience that maintains context across Google’s products.

Sharing Of Contextual Data The sharing of personal and conversational context across Google’s products enables users to continue activities without having to start over.

Expansion Beyond Information Discovery The integration of additional data sources enables Google to become increasingly useful for planning, decision-making, and accomplishing tasks.

Increasingly Personalized Search Experiences Search responses are becoming more specific to individual users, a change that SEOs need to really think about and integrate into how what they do fits into this new multi-dimensional level of Search.

How To Opt Out Of Google Personal Intelligence Google is giving users greater insight into and control over the personal context used to generate AI Mode responses. Users can opt out or in from Personal Intelligence here.

Google Search is increasingly an experience that’s as much about what Google knows about the user and what they want to accomplish as it is about what the user is searching for. This is arguably one of the most consequential moments in SEO that I have experienced in my nearly 30 years of experience in SEO.
